SINCE LATE NOVEMBER THE WAR HAS BEEN IN A TWILIGHT PERIOD OF 
RELATIVELY LIGHT ACTION. 

IT WAS STILL TOO EARLY TO TELL WHETHER THE CURRENT FLURRY OF 
FIGHTING WAS PORTENTOUS OR WAS MERELY ANOTHER OF THE SHORT SPURTS 
TAKEN FROM TIME TO TIME WHILE THE TRUCE NEGOTIATORS HAGGLED. 

THE ALLIES, HOWEVER, EVIDDENTLY WERE TAKING A STRONGER INTEREST IN 
WHAT THE CHINESE AND NORTH KOREAN REDS WERE UP TO. 

THE POWERFUL COMMUNIST OFFENSIVES OF LAST APRIL AND MAY ARE 
WELL REMEMBERED, AND UeSe EIGHTH ARMY OFFICERS BELIEVE TTHE REDS 
ARE CAPABLE OF ANOTHER OFFENSIVE THIS SPRING. 

THIS DESPITE THE EFFECTIVENESS OF THE AIR FORCES’ SIX MONTHS OF 
"OPERATION STRANGLE,” AIMED AT DESTROYING RED COMMUNICATIONS AND 
SUPPLY BASES THROUGHOUT NORTH KOREA. 

ALLIED TANK THRUSTS FRIDAY WEST OF CHORWON AND AROUND KUMSONG 
ON THE CENTRAL FRONT COST AT LEAST 10 TANKS DESTROYED OR DAMAGED BY 
THE VIOLENT RED RESPONSE. AT LEAST 15 COMMUNIST DEFENSIVE BUNKERS 
WERE LISTED AS DESTROYED OR DAMAGED. 

A TANK-INFANTRY TEAM SATURDAY HIT THE REDS SOUTH OF PYONGGANG, PEAK 
OF THE OLD "IRON TRIANGLE* AREA ON THE CENTRAL FRONT. TWO ALLIED TANKS 
WERE DAMAGED BUT RECOVERED IN THE ONE AND ONE-HALF HOUR RAID. 

THE RAID IN THE PYONGGANG SECTOR MARKED THE FIRST TIME IN WEEKS THAT 
THE ALLIES HAVE TESTED THAT AREA WITH TANKS. IT WAS IN THE VALLEY

FOR THE BETTER.

IN THE SAME VEIN, HE TOLD THE ASSOCIATED PRESS TODAY: 

“THERE ARE SOME PEOPLE WHO STILL ENTERTAIN A HOPE THAT POLITICAL 
OR DIPLOMATIC MEANS OF SETTLING THE PROBLEM WOULD BE BETTER THAN

BUT RHEE SAID HE FELT SUCH VIEWS DENOTED A LACK OF UNDERSTANDING 
OF COMMUNISM'’S GOALS. 

"I HAVE SEEN BILATERAL CONFERENCES ON UNIFICATION FAIL IN THE PAST," 
RHEE SAID. "AND I ALSO HAVE OBSERVED THE SAME FAILURES ON THE DIPLO}- 
MATIC LEVEL IN THE UNITED NATIONS. I AM SORELY PUZZLED AS TO WHAT NEW 
POLITICAL AND DIPLOMATIC METHODS WILL BE OR CAN BE EMPLOYED AT THIS 
TIME WHICH WILL BE SUCCESSFUL." ayy 

HE REITERATED: 

"ANY SOLUTION SHORT OF COMPLETE UNIFICATION OF KOREA CANNOT BE 
CONSIDERED AS A SOLUTION AT ALL. 

"IF THE CHINESE COMMUNIST FORCES ARE EITHER PERSUADED OR FORCED TO 
EVACUATE OUR TERRITORY, WE WILL CONSIDER IT AS COMPLETION OF UNIFICATT- 
ION AND WILL ACCEPT IT’AS A SOLUTION." 

HE MADE EVIDENT THAT BY "OUR TERRITORY" HE MEANT ALL OF KOREA. 

"T AM SURE." HE CONTINUED, "THAT IF THE U.N. WILL KEEP ON FIGHTING 
THEM (THE SHINES F} AND AT THE SAME TIME GIVE THEM SUFFICIENT ASSURANCE 
THAT WE WILL NOT ATTACK THEM IN THEIR OWN TERRITORY, THEN THE U.Ne 
MAY SUCCEED." 

HE INDICATED THAT HE BELIEVED THE SOUTH KOREANS THEMSELVES THEN 
COULD UNIFY THE COUNTRY IF GIVEN ENOUGH ARMS AND TRAINING.

TUESDAY MARCH 4=-(AP)-SOVIET NEWSPAPERS REPORTED TODAY THAT 
MORE DRASTIC MEASURES ARE BEING TAKEN IN NORTH KOREA AGAINST THE 
CURRENT PLAGUE EPIDEMIC THERE, 

“PRAVDA PUBLISHED A TASS DISPATCH FROM PYONGYANG, NORTH KOREAN 
CAPITAL, SAYING A SPECIAL ORDER OF THE WAR COMMITTEE OF THE NORTH 
KOREAN GOVERNMENT HAD ORDERED THAT ALL OF NORTH KOREA'S ARMED FORCES 
AND CIVILIAN POPULATION BE INOCULATED AGAINST THE PLAGUE. THE ORDER 
WAS SIGNED BY KIM IL SUNG. 

THE DECREE ALSO ORDERED THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND THE CHIEF OF 
ADMINISTRATION OF THE MILITARY MEDICAL SERVICE TO MAKE SURE MILITIA 
UNITS ARE USED IN FIGHTING THE EPIDEMIC. 

SHIPMENTS OF FOOD, CLOTHING, AND OTHER ARTICLES FROM QUARANTINED 
DISTRICTS WERE FORBIDDEN. A GENERAL WAR ON RATS AND OTHER RODENTS SAID | 
TO BE CARRIERS OF THE DISEASE WAS ORDERED. THE SOVIET PRESS PREVIOUSLY 5 
HAS SAID THE EPIDEMIC IS BUBONIC PLAGUE. CARRIED BY RATS. —. 

THE NORTH KOREAN ORDER AGAIN BLAMED THE EPIDEMIC ON "AMERICAN a 
BACTERIOLOGICAL WARFARE."

"YOU CANNOT GET A 15 PER CENT TAX INCREASE THROUGH PARLIAMENT,"

FOR EUROPE'S DEFENSE, THAT WAS OUTLINED AT LISBON, CAN BE REALIZED.

IN WASHINGTON. SECRETARY OF STATE DEAN ACHESON FACED SHARP 
QUESTIONING ON THE FRENCH POLITICAL SITUATION BEFORE THE SENATE

FAILURE TO VOTE TAXES TO SUPPORT HER NATO OBLIGATIONS, WITH SOME 
THREATENING PRIVATELY TO VOTE FOR AN END TO AMERICAN AID TO FRANCE 

NLESS THE PROBLEM IS SOLVED QUICKLY. 

FRANCE'S SHARE OF UeS. AID FOR THE YEAR ENDING JUNE 30 HAS BEEN 
SET AT 600 MILLION DOLLARS. 

FRANCE IS BESET WITH A TWO-FRONT MILITARY PROBLEM -- THE FIGHTING 
OF A REAL WAR IN INDOCHINA AND THE PREPARATION OF HER DEFENSES IN 
WESTERN EUROPE AGAINST POSSIBLE COMMUNIST AGGRESSION. f 


A114 
| SHE IS SPENDING ABOUT 1 1/2 BILLION DOLLARS FOR THE INDOCHINA 
WAR AND HAS BEEN ASKED TO NEARLY DOUBLE THAT FIGURE FOR EUROPEAN 
DEFENSE. THIS COMES AT A TIME WHEN THE VALUE OF THE FRANC IS 
DECREASING, MAKING PURCHASES OF MILITARY EQUIPMENT MORE COSTLY ALL 
THE TIME. 

CONFRONTED WITH THE GOVERNMENTAL CRISIS, SOME AMERICAN AND FRENCH 
OFFICIALS ARE GIVING SERIOUS CONSIDERATION FOR THE FIRST TIME TO 
GIVING UP IN INDOCHINA AND LETTING THE COMMUNISTS TAKE OVER» | 

THIS WOULD BE A GRAVE DECISION AND NO DOUBT WOULD CALL FOR 
CONFERENCES ON THE HIGHEST LEVELS. GIVING UP INDOCHINA MIGHT PUT 
THE COMMUNISTS IN CONTROL IN THAILAND, MALAYA, BURMA AND POSSIBLY 
INDIA. THE OFFICIAL FRENCH GOVERNMENT POSITION IS TO HANG ON, BU 
THE COUNTRY IS WEARY OF WAGING A WAR THAT IS YET INCONCLUSIVE WITH 
NO END IN SIGHT. 

BUT OF IMMEDIATE CONCERN WAS THE POLITICAL CRISIS WHICH STALLED 
DEVELOPMENT OF THE WESTERN EUROPEAN DEFENSE PLANS AND MAY CALL FOR 
THEIR RECASTING.

BONN, GERMANY, MARCH 3-(AP)-WEST GERMANY HAS COMPLAINED THAT THE 
FRENCH=BACKED GOVERNMENT OF THE DISPUTED $ SIN IS CONSTANTLY

NEIGHBOR OVER THE COAL-RICH BORDER TERRITORY WITH A NOTE OF COMPLAINT 
TO THE EUROPEAN ASSEMBLY. A CHIEF CHARGE IS THAT THE SAAR GOVERNMENT 
HAS STIFLED A PRO-GERMAN POLITICAL OPPOSITION PARTY. 

COUNTRIES CONNECTED WITH THE EUROPEAN ASSEMBLY--AN UNOFFICIAL 13- 
NATION PARLIAMENT WITHOUT ACTUAL POWER--ARE PLEDGED TO RESPECT BASIC 
HUMAN RIGHTS. THE FRENCH-INFLUENCED SAAR GOVERNMENT IS AN ASSOCIATE 
MEMBER OF THE ASSEMBLY. | 

GERMAN INFORMANTS SAID CHANCELLOR KONRAD ADENAUER WOULD RAISE THE 
SAAR ISSUE AT THE MEETING MARCH 19 IN PARIS OF THE ASSEMBLY'S COMMITTEE 
OF MINISTERS, ITS CONTROLLING UPPER HOUSE.

BONN GERMANY, MARCH 3-C(AP9-THE WEST GERMAN GOVERNMENT HAS 
COMPLETED THE DRAFT OF A OUTLAWING CAR AND MONOPOLIES 
GOVERNMENT OFFICIALS SAID TODAY. IT WILL BE SENT TO PARLIAMENT AFTER 
ITS FINAL APPROVAL, PROBABLY NEXT WEEK. 
PREPARED BY GERMAN EXPERTS IN CONSULTATION WITH THE ALLIED HIGH 


COMMISSION, THE BILL WOULD FORBID THE FORMATION OF CARTELS, ; COMBINES, 
SYNDICATES AND OTHER TYPES OF MONOPOLISTIC ARRANGEMENTS WHEN THE 
ALLIED OCCUPATION ENDS. 

IT WILL SUPERSEDE PRESENT ALLIED ANTI-TRUST LAWS IN GERMANY. THE NEU 
BILL DOES NOT DEAL WITH SPECIFIC ALLIED TRUST-BREAKING PROGRAMS 
SUCH AS THE REORGANIZATION OF THE BIG RUHR COAL AND STEEL INDUSTRIES. 

IF THESE SPECIFIC PROGRAMS ARE STILL INCOMPLETE WHEN THE ALLIED 
OCCUPATION ENDS, THE GERMANS WILL AGREE TO PUSH THEM To 
COMPLETION, ALLIED OFFICIALS SAID. 

THE GERMAN ANTI-TRUST BILL PROVIDES FOR FINES UP TO A MILLION MARKS 
($238,000) FOR VIOLATIONS. IT EXEMPTS THE NATIONAL BANK, STATE CENTRAL 
BANKS, RECONSTRUCTION ORGANIZATIONS AND THE FEDERAL RAILWAY SYSTEM.

IS SEARCHING FOR ANY SUBVERSIVE INFLUENCES ON U.S.» POLICIES IN THE FAR 
EAST. THE INVESTIGATION HAS CENTERED ON THE IPR, A PRIVATE RESEARCH 
ORGANIZATION OF WHICH LATTIMORE IS A TRUSTEE. 

WHEN TODAY'S SESSION WAS CUT SHORT BY LEGISLATIVE ACTION IN THE 
SENATE, LATTIMORE, A JOHNS HOPKINS UNIVERSITY PROFESSOR AND FAR EASTERN 
AFFAIRS SPECIALIST, WAS DIRECTED TO RETURN TOMORROW. 

LATTIMORE SERVED AS AN ADVISER TO CHIANG KAISHEK, THE CHINESE NATION= 
ALIST LEADER, IN 1941 AND 1942 ON THE NOMINATION OF THE LATE PRESIDEN 

HE FIRST TESTIFIED THAT HIS RECOLLECTION WAS THAT HIS LUNCHEON WITH 
OUMANSKY WAS AFTER THE GERMAN INVASION OF RUSSIA. HE ALSO SAID THAT AT 
THE TIME THERE HAD BEEN A GOOD DEAL OF PUBLICITY ABOUT HIS APPOINTMENT 
AS AN ADVISER TO CHIANG AND SPECULATION ABOUT ITS EXACT NATURE. 

THE SUBCOMMITTEE ESTABLISHED THROUGH VARIOUS DOCUMENTS THAT THE 
LUNCHEON WAS HELD ON JUNE 13 AND THAT THE LIBRARY OF CONGRESS HAD 
FOUND THAT THE ANNOUNCEMENT OF LATTIMORE'S APPOINTMENT AS AN ADVISER 
THE CHINESE GENERALISSINO CARRIED IN THE NEW YORK TIMES OF 
LATTIMORE SAID THIS EVIDENCE "SHOW MY R ECTION WAS I! TEe® 
HE ADDED, HOWEVER, THAT A NUMBER OF PERSONS KNEW ABOUT HIS ASSIGNMENT 
BEFORE IT WAS MADE PUBLIC.

(300) CHAMBER-COMMUNISM 
-WASMINGTON, MARCH 3-(AP)-THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED 
STATES SAYS THE BEST WAY TO KILL_THE COMMUNIST PARTY IN THIS COUNTRY 
IS TO "STARVE" IT TO DEATH FINANCIALLY AND CUT OFF ITS SOURCES OF ‘POW- 


ER. 

IT SAID THIS COULD BE DONE BY REFUSING=@@MMUNISTS JOBS IN VIRTUALLY 
ALL BRANCHES OF INDUSTRY, AND CHOKING OFF PRESTIGE, POWER AND HIGH 
SALARIES BY FREEZING THEM OUT OF THE ENTERTAINMENT, NEWSPAPER, RADIO 
AND SIMILAR FIELDS. 

THE CHAMBER ALSO SHARPLY CRITICIZED U.sS. FOREIGN POLICY IN A REPORT 
PREPARED BY ITS COMMITTEE ON COMMUNISM, RELEASED YESTERDAY. 

"IT WOULD NOT BE TOO HARD, IF WE ALL WORKED AT IT. TO STARVE IT 
(THE COMMUNIST PARTY) FINANCIALLY AND LEAVE IT A DISORGANIZED GROUP 
OF POWERLESS FANATICS," THE REPORT SAID. 

"IF EVERY SOURCE OF FUNDS AND POWER WERE SYSTEMATICALLY CUT OFF, 
THE PARTY WOULD BE WEAKENED TO THE POINT OF EXTINCTION," 

POINTING OUT THAT IT IS PUBLIC POLICY NOT TO HIRE COMMUNISTS FOR 
GOVERNMENT JOBS, IT SAID PRIVATE BUSINESS SHOULD FOLLOW A SIMILAR POL- 
ICY AND NOT EMPLOY COMMUNISTS "AND THE VARIOUS FRINGES OF FELLOW TRAV- 
ELERS AND DUPES." 

IT SUGGESTED THAT COMMUNISTS SHOULD NOT BE HIRED IN: 

"ANY PLANT LARGE ENOUGH TO HAVE A LABOR UNION; ANY SCHOOL OR -UNI- 
VERSITY; ANY AGENCY WHICH INFLUENCES PUBLIC OPINION, SUCH AS NEWS- 
PAPERS, RADIO, TELEVISION, BOOK AND MAGAZINE PUBLISHING AND RESEARCH 
INSTITUTIONS; AND ANY FIELD WHICH GIVES PRESTIGE AND HIGH SALARIES TO 
COMMUNISTS, SUCH AS THE ENTERTAINMENT FIELD.® 

THE CHAMBER SAID "NO EXCUSES" SHOULD BE OFFERED FOR THIS ATTITUDE. 

"IT IS NOT PENALIZING PERSONS FOR THEIR ‘POLITICAL’ VIEWS. IT IS 
SIMPLY DENYING INDIRECT FINANCIAL AID TO A MOVEMENT WHICH IS ESSEN- 
TIALLY TREASON." 

REGARDING FOREIGN POLICY, THE REPORT MADE THESE COMMENTSS 

"IT IS DIFFICULT TO DRAW THE LINE BETWEEN TREASON AND BLUNDERING®

P MARCH 4-CAP)-TRANSPORT MINISTER ANTOINE_PINAY TODAY URGED 
FRANCE TO BACK HIM IN SEEKING A~ROLIZTICAL TRUCE AND A GOVERNMENT

"IT 1§ NECESSARY. TO FORM A MINISTRY FOR DEFENSE OF THE FRANC WITH THE

A BILLION FRANCS ($2,800,000) IS LEAKING FROM THE TREASURY 
DAILY TO PAY FOR THINGS PARLIAMENT HAS APPROVED, BUT FOR WHICH IT HAS 
NOT YET VOTED FUNDS. INFLATION IS MOUNTING, 

PINAY TOLD HIS COLLEAGUES AT THE NATIONAL ASSEMBLY LATE TODAY 
HE WOULD PRESENT HIMSELF THURSDAY FOR CONFIRMATION AS PREMIER, BUT 
HE BACK=TRACKED AFTER HE HAD A 45-MINUTE TALK WITH PRESIDENT 
VINCENT AURIOL AT THE PRESIDENTIAL PALACE. ON LEAVING THE PALACE, 

HE SAID HE WOULD NOT YET MAKE UP HIS MIND ABOUT HIS APPEARANCE 
FOR CONFIRMATION. 

THIS IMMEDIATELY CAUSED SPECULATION THAT AURIOL, HIMSELF A SOCIALIST, 
WAS WORRIED ABOUT THE PLAN OF PINAY, AN INDEPENDENT REPUBLICAN, TO GIVE 
THE NATION ITS FIRST RIGHT-WING GOVERNMENT SINCE BEFORE THE WAR. 

WHEN PINAY TALKED WITH AURIOL, HE HAD PLEDGES OF SUPPORT ONLY FROM 
RIGHT WING GROUPS, 

IF THIS ASSUMPTION IS TRUE, PINAY UNDOUBTEDLY WILL SPEND THE 
INTERVAL TRYING TO LINE UP SUPPORT AMONG THE LEFTIST POPULAR 
REPUBLICAN MOVEMENT (MRP) AND THE SOCIALISTS. UP TO NOW, THE 
SOCIALISTS HAVE REFUSED TO ENTER A CABINET WITH THE CONSERVATIVE 


FOLLOWERS OF GEN.CHARLES DE GAULLE, THE RALLY OF THE FRENCH PEOPLE 
(RPF), THE BIGGEST PARTY IN THE ASSEMBLY. 

WHEN HE FACES PARLIAMENT, PINAY WILL NEED AT LEAST 313 VOTES TO 
BE FORMALLY INVESTED AS PREMIER, THIS WILL BE ONLY HALF THE BATTLE, 
HOWEVER. IF HE IS CONFIRMED, HE MUST THEN PUT A CABINET TOGETHER 
TO SATISFY ALL THE VARIOUS ELEMENTS WHICH VOTED TO GIVE HIM THE JO

THE ALASKAN=BASED F-9h GROUP HAS A NEW MISSION: TO PROTECT ALASKAN 
AIRFIELDS FROM BOMBER STRIKES OR SEIZURE BY RUSSIAN AIRBORNE FORCES 
AND TO INTERCEPT ANY LONG-RANGE RUSSIAN BOMBER INTENT ON STRIKING AT

THE F-94 IS A TWO-PLACE PLANE CARRYING A PILOT AND A RADAR OBSERVER. 
THE LATTER’S JOB IS TO LOCATE ON HIS RADAR“SCOPE THE GENERAL DIRECTION 
OF AN ENEMY PLANE, THEN GUIDE THE PILOT TO A POINT WHERE HE CAN LOCATE 

PLANE ON HIS RABAR GUN-SIGHT AND CLOSE IN FOR THE KILL. 
IN ALASKA AND ELSEWHERE, INTERCEPTOR PLANE UNITS WORK DIRECTLY WITH 
THE RADAR NETWORKS WHICH CiVE EARLY WARNING OF THE APPROACH OF UNIDEN- 

THE LOCKHEED ANNOUNCEMENT, EMPHASIZING THE STATE OF ALERTNESS OF AIR 
DEFENSE IN THE STRATEGIC NORTH (WHICH LOOKS OUT UPON THE POLAR PATHS 
ALONG WHICH RUSSIAN AERIAL INVADERS MIGHT COME) SAYS THE F-94S ARE 
SPOTTED 24 HOURS A DAY ON RUNWAYS, READY FOR INSTANT TAKEOFF. | 

POWER CARTS, TO KEEP INSTRUMENTS ENERGIZED AND TO START THE JET 
ENGINES QUICKLY, STAND ALONGSIDE THE PLANES. IN A "READY SHACK,® CREWS

LOCKHEED AIRCRAFT CORP,, MAKERS OF THE F-94 INTERCEPTOR JETS, _ 
ANNOUNCED THIS LAST NIGHT, WITH PERMISSION OF THE AIR FORCE. 

THE ANNOUNCEMENT SAID F-94'S ARE NOW OPERATING UNDER THE ALASKAN 
AIR COMMAND IN THE 57TH FIGHTER-INTERCEPTOR GROUP. IN REPLY TO QUERIES, 
THE AIR FORCE SAID THE EQUIVALENT OF A GROUP--NORMALLY 36 PLANES-~ 
OF THE ALL-VEATHER JETS IS Nov BASED IN JAPAN AS PART OF THE 13TH 
AIR FORCE. 

THEIR MISSIONS: IN JAPAN, TO PROTECT AMERICAN INSTALLATIONS FROM 
ANY SUDDEN ATTACK BY RED FORCES, EITHER THOSE OF CHINA OR THE 
SOVIET UNION. IN ALASKA, TO GUARD AGAINST ANY RUSSIAN BOMBING STRIKE 
OR AIRBORNE SEIZURE OF ALASKAN AIRFIELDS AND TO INTERCEPT ANY LONG- 
RANGE INVASION ALONG THE POLAR PATH FROM RUSSIA TO THE UNITED STATES. 

THE F-94 IS A TWO-SEATER, CARRYING A PILOT AND A RADAR OBSERVER. 

ON HIS RADARSCOPE IN THE PLANE, THE OBSERVER LOCATES AN ENEMY CRAFT | 

AND GUIDES THE PILOT TO A POINT WHERE HIS RADAR-POINTED GUNS CAN MAKE Ti 

KILL. 

LOCKHEED'S ANNOUNCEMENT EMPHASIZED THE STATE OF ALERTNESS OF AIR 

DEFENSE IN THE STRATEGIC NORTH. IT SAID F-94'S ARE SPOTTED CONSTANTLY 

ON RUNWAYS, READY FOR INSTANT TAKE OFF. CREWS, FULLY DRESSED IN ARC- 
TAND B 

GROUND RADARS SIGNAL THE APPROACH OF AN UNIDENTIFIED PLANE, 

THE JETS KITE FOR IT--EVEN IF IT ONLY TURNS OUT TO BE A STRAGGLING 

BUSH PILOT OR AN AIRLINER STRAYING OFF COURSE.

MILITARY ESTABLISHMENT IN COMPARISON WITH THE UNITED STATES, HOWEV 

THIS IS BECAUSE OF A VASTLY LOWER STANDARD OF LIVING IN THE SOVTE 
UNION, LOWER PAY TO THE SOVIET SOLDIER, MUCH CHEAPER PRODUCTION COST 
BECAUSE OF MUCH FORCED LABOR, PROCUREMENT IN DOMINATED SATELLITE 
COUNTRIES AT FAVORABLE RATES. AND OTHER FACTORS SUCH AS A CONTROLLED 
ECONOMY AND HIDDEN MILITARY EXPENSES. |

EISENHOWER AND GRUENTHER ARE ON A TOUR TO GET ACQUAINTED WITH 
TURKEY AND GREECE, THE NEWEST MEMBERS OF THE NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY 
ORGANIZATION. THEY WERE TOLD TODAY GREECE HAS THE EQUIVALENT OF 
43 DIVISIONS, RATHER THAN THE GENERALLY ESTIMATED 10. 

THE EXTRA OUTFITS ARE A COMMANDO DIVISION IN A COMBAT READY 
STATUS AND TWO INFANTRY DIVISIONS READY EXCEPT FOR SUPPORT WEAPONS, 
WHICH ARE DUE FROM THE UNITED STATES. GREEK DIVISIONS RUN ABOUT 
10,000 MEN EACH, LESS THAN IN MOST NATO COUNTRIES.

THE COMMUNIST PARTY IS OUTLAWED IN LEBANON, BUT THE TOLERANT | 
LEBANESE GOVERNMENT GIVES INDIVIDUAL COMMUNISTS AMPLE OPPORTUNITY TO 
WORK. IN THE LAST ELECTIONS, KNOWN COMMUNISTS APPEARED ON THE 
BALLOT AS INDEPENDENTS. THE COMMUNISTS HAVE A WELL-DISCIPLINED 
NATIONAL ORGANIZATION, WITH DISTRICT AND LOCAL COMMITTEES. SINCE 
LEBANON WAS THE LAST ARAB STATE TO OUTLAW THE PARTY, COMMUNISTS ARE 
BETTER ORGANIZED HERE THAN IN THE REST OF THE ARAB LEAGUE 

COMMUNIST STRENGTH APPEARS TO BE INCREASING IN THE LEBANESE LABOR 
MOVEMENT. ALTHOUGH THE COMMUNIST GROUP, ACCORDING TO RELIABLE REPORTS, 
ENCOMPASSES ONLY FOUR UNIONS TO THE GOVERNMENT LEAGUE'S 23. BEST 
ESTIMATES INDICATE THAT COMMUNISTS NOW CONTROL 10,000 OUT OF AN 
ESTIMATED 25,000 ORGANIZED WORKERS. 

THE COMMUNISTS ARE MAKING THEIR BIGGEST GAINS AMONG THE SO-CALLED 
"FRINGE" WORKERS -- NORMALLY LEFT OUT OF THE MORE ORTHODOX TRADE 
UNIONS. AMONG THESE AR LEATHER AND TEXTILE WORKERS, STEVEDORES AND 
LAUNDRYMEN. COMMUNISTS ALSO ARE BELIEVED TO CONTROL THE POWERFUL 
UNION OF TRANSPORT AND LAND COMMUNICATIONS. 

IN ADDITION TO THEIR WORK AMONG UNIONS, LEBANESE COMMUNISTS ARE 
CREDITED WITH SIGNIFICANT PROPAGANDA GAINS IN THE "PARTISANS OF 
PEACE” MOVEMENT. AGITATION FOR NATIONALIZATION OF FOREIGN CONCESSIONS 
AND, 10 A LESSER DEGREE, WITHIN THE MEMBERSHIP OF THE RUSSIAN ORTHODOX 

THE "PARTISANS OF PEACE" GOT 60,000 LEBANESE SIGNATURES FOR THE 
STOCKHOLM PEACE PETITION OUT OF A TOTAL POPULATION OF 1,200,000 (M). 
LEADERS OF THE LEBANESE GROUP ARE IN CLOSE TOUCH WITH EUROPEAN 
COMMUNIST LEADERSAND TOOK AN ACTIVE PART IN THE WORLD PEACE 
CONFERENCE IN VIENNA LAST FALL.

democratic hope may be extermi- 
nated in broad areas of this earth. 
If we rise to our historic tradi- 
tions, we can add powerful momen- 
tum to the democratic counter-of- 


fensive which inspires in the people 
‘of the world a sense of their own 
‘destiny as free men—and which 
will in the end burst the bonds of 
tyranny everywhere on earth. 
| The pursuit of mutual security’ 
through mufual strength is thus) 
‘the keystone of the broad foreign) 
‘policy which the United States and) 
jother free nations have adopted as| 
the surest road to lasting peace. 
The American péople have stead- 
fastly supported this foreign pol- 
iey since the second World War. 
Its pattern today is sharp and 
clear. If I were to make a brief; 
definition of our policy, I would| 
icall it the policy of peace through 
i\collective strength. | 
_ We are joined with other coun-| 
tries in the patient and systematic 
‘building in the free world of 
‘enough military strength to defer 
‘external Communist aggression: 
‘and of economic and political and 
‘moral strength to remove internal 
‘threats of Communist subversion 
and point the way toward demo- 
cratic progress. 
I wish tqemphasize very strong- 
ly that all these forms of strength 
- are necessary if we are to achieve 
freedom and peace. The plain and 
inescapable fact is that they are 
indivisible. Neither military 
strength nor economic strength nor 
\political strength nor moral 
strength can do the job alone. 
| Military strength is the first ne- 
icessity, for without a shield 
lagainst aggression the free world 
‘would be helpless before the en- 
‘emy. Military strength must be 


built, and we must help build it, 
in Europe and in other critical 
areas of the world. But military 
strength is not just a matter of 
idelivering arms to our allies. It 
‘is also a matter of defense sup- 
|port to enable our allies to lo 
‘more to expand and equip their 
‘own defense forces, 
_ And even arms and defense sup- 
port together do not provide a full 
‘answer to the Soviet threat; to be- 
lieve that they do is dangerously 
to misunderstand the nature of the 
foe. The gun is but one weapon in 
‘the Soviet arsenal of aggression. 
If we ignored the necessity for 
‘building moral and political and 
economic strength, we would ex- 
pose ourselves to the danger of 
\Communist gains which could be 
at least as damaging as outright 
jaggression. Since the Soviet Union 
does not rely exclusively on mili- 
tary attack, we would be foolish 
indeed to rely exclusively on mili- 
itary defense. 


Outline of the Program 
| The funds required under the 


‘Mutual Security Program fall into 
‘two broad categories. 

| The first of these, which is by 
far the larger, is for assistance in 
\building up the military strength 
of friendly nations. This aid is of 
two types: (1) direct military aid, 
primarily in the form of military 
equipment and components there- 
of, and (2) defense support—pri- 
marily in the form of raw mate- 
rials, commodities, and machinery 
—to enable other countries to sus- 
tain and increase their military 
efforts, where that type of sup- 
port produces greater returns in 
military strength than would an 
equal amount of direct military 
aid. 

The bulk of the direct military 

aid and of the defense support will 
go to strengthen the defenses of 
the free nations in Europe. 
Amounts for direct military aid 
and defense support make up 
about 90 per cent of the total 
funds recomgnended for the Mu- 
tual Security Program for the fis- 
cal year 1953. 
The second broad category is 
for economic and technical assist- 
ance, primarily for the under- 
developed areas of the world, 
where economic progress is the 
first essential in the battle for 
freedom. Some of these funds 
will in fact also support defense 
efforts in certain countries in 
Southeast Asia, where Commu- 
nist aggression is an immediate 
menace. Amounts recommended 
for economic and technical assist- 
ance are about 10 per cent of the 
total. 

The distribution of the amounts 
recommended is shown in more de- 
‘tail in the following table:

| In the Mutual Security Act oi 
\1951, the Congress provided for 
‘an integrated program, adminis- 
‘tered by appropriate operating 
agencies under the general direc- 
‘tion of the Director for Mutual 
‘Security. These arrangements are 
working well, and I recommend 
‘that they be continued. Under 
ithem, direct military aid will be 
‘administered by the Department 
‘of Defense. 
_ The Mutual Security Agency 
\will administer defense support in 
Europe, together with technical 
‘and economic assistance in South- 
‘east Asia and the Pacific. In South 
‘Asia, the Near East, Latin Amer- 
‘ica, and the independent states of 
Africa, economic and technical as- 
sistance will be administered by 
the Technical Cooperation Admin- 
istration of the Department of 
‘State. 

We shall continue our policy of 
‘closely coordinating the Mutual 
Security program with the techni- 
‘cal assistance programs of the or- 
iganization of American states and 
‘the United Nations and its agen- 
cies, such as the food and agricul- 
ture organization and the world 
health organization. In addition, 
we shall continue to encourage, to 
the maximum extent possible, the 
investment of private capital for 
economic development abroad, and 
we shall continue to relate outlays 
under the Mutual Security Pro- 
gram to the loans being made by 
the Export-Import Bank and the 
Internatonal Bank for Reconstruc- 
tion and Development.

;|They require further progress to- 


way to a solution. The last five 
years have recorded remarkable 
gains as a result of action we have 
taken under our policy of peace 
through collective strength—first 
in Greece and Turkey; then, in 
1948, through the European Re- 
covery Program, and since 1949 
through the growing defensive 
power of the North Atlantic Treaty 
Organization. The American con- 
tribution did not of itself create 
these gains; but it did supply the 
essential margin without which the 
Europeans could not have fought 
their way out of their postwar 
slough of despond. » 

Five years ago, many European 
nations were on the verge of eco- 
nomie or political collapse. A. 
divided and despairing continent— 
next to our own, the most pro-' 
ductive and industrially powerful 
in the world—lay open for Soviet 
|conquest. 

How different the picture is to- 
day! Europe has made immense 
advances—in economic output, in 
military strength, in political self- 
confidence, in progress toward 
|unity. Today the Soviet Union 
knows that it cannot achieve its 
purposes in Europe, so long as the 
policy of collective strength con- 
tinues. 

Europe still has far to go. Eco- 
nomic health and vitality in Europe 
require a series of specific actions 
—varying from country to country 
—to raise industrial and agricul- 
tural productivity, to knock down 
trade barriers and exchange re- 
strictions. and to encourage the 


vigorous forces of competition in 
-|European and world markets. 


-|ward the democratic goals of a 
fair distribution of income, strong 
‘and free trade unions, fair and 
‘effective tax systems, and pro- 
grams of land reform. 

_ Above all, we in the United 
‘States do not believe that Western 
‘Europe can achieve its full 
strength without accelerated prog- 
‘ress toward unity. Only this unity 
can release the great potential 
energy of free Europe, We will 
continue in every way we can to 
encourage its attainment. 

The difficulties are very great. 
‘It is only candid to report that 
progress in this direction has not 
always been as fast as we hoped. 
Yet in many respects the prog- 
ress has been most impressive. 

_ A revolution has been taking’ 
place in European thinking. The 
Organization for European Eco- 
nomic Cooperation and the Euro- 
pean Payments Union have laid 
‘foundations for joint action in the 
economic and financial fields. In the 
‘Schuman Plan, six countries are, 
creating an international author- 
ity for the production and distri- 
bution of coal and steel. Under the 


European defense community, the 


30.24- 


same six countries are planning to 
establish a common armed forces, 
a common defense ministry and a 
common military budget. 

Europe has moved faster toward 
integration in the last five vears 
than it did in the previous 500. At 
‘every stage in this movement the 
‘United States has provided encour- 
agement and support. If this prog- 
‘ress continues in the next five 
-years—and I am confident it will— 
a new Europe will emerge as a 
great and creative partner in the 
defense of freedom. 


Build-up Is Encouraging 


It is this progress toward Euro- 
/pean economic recovery and politi- 
cal unity which makes possible a 
\growing defense effort in Western 
Europe. The build-up of military 
Strength there since the signing of 
‘the North Atlantic Treaty has 
‘been most encouraging. In the 
‘coming fiscal year, European mili- 
tary expenditures will be consid- 
erably more than twice as large 
as they were in the year preceding 
the Communist aggression in 
Korea. 

Production of military matériel 
in Western Europe has multiplied 
about four times in that period. 
The European nations have length- 
ened the training periods under 
their compulsory military serv- 
ice programs and have substan- 
tially enlarged and improved their 
armed forces. The pace of the mil- 
itary buiid-up has given many mil- 
lions of Europeans new confidence 
in their capacity to resist aggres- 
sion. 

This is an impressive record of 
progress. Of course, the record is 
far from perfect — especially in| 
view of the urgency of the threat 
posed by aggressive Soviet impe- 
rialism. We can find many specific 
weaknesses and shortcomings to 
criticize—and some people in our 
country fasten their attention so 
exclusively on such things as to 


advocate that the defense of Eu- 
rope be abandoned. 

| I do not wish to minimize the 
‘shortcomings, but the fyundamen- 
tal question to ask is: “Are we 
jmoving at a substantial rate in 
‘the right direction? Is real prog, 
‘ress being made?" The answer 
‘is obvious. So is the conclusion to 


|be drawn, The record abundantly 


warrants confidence in our FEuro- 
‘pean Allies, and our continued 
.Steadfast support for them. 

Two weeks ago, at Lisbon, the 


‘member nations took the most far- 


reaching strides in European de- 
fense since the adoption of the 
North Atlantic Treaty itself in 
1949. The North Atlantic Council 
at Lisbon endorsed the specific 


means through which the forces 


of the European defeiise com- 
munity—including German 
{tingents—wilt be organized and 
iti into General senhower's 
command, 

After months of planning by the 
special committee under the chair. 
manship of Mr, Harriman, the 
(council made specific and concrete 
decisions providing for the more 
rapid build-up of forces and for 

the provision of the necessar; 
equipment and construction tc 
‘support them. 

By the end of this calendar year, 
General Eisenhower's command is 
expected to have at its disposal a 
formidable force—including some 
fifty Army divisions, about half of 
them on active duty, and some 
4,000 military planes—and a sound 
base for further build-up in 1953 
and 1954, These forces, joined by 
those of Greece and Turkey, will 
bring within measurable distance 
the time when even the most fool- 
hardy man in the Kremlin will not 
dare risk open attack. 

In order to equip the forces be- 
ing raised by our Allies under the 
‘Lisbon agreements, we, as well as 
they, must step up our efforts. 
‘There have been delays in our own 
production and delivery of arms. 
And combat requirements for Ko- 
rea have, of course, received top 
priority for deliveries from our 
current output. I am sure that 
production is now being accelerated 
substantially, and I have conse- 
quently directed that deliveries to 
the North Atlantic Treaty defense 
forces be greatly speeded up. 


Thé Problems of Europe 


The rearmament effort has also 
created problems in Europe. The 
European economy, after its ex- 
traordinary comeback in the years 
of the European recovery pro- 
gram has now been subjected to 
new and severe pressures. The 
Marshall Plan was designed to 
help restore minimum economic) 
health, not to produce a surplus: 
capable of creating military forces 
adequate for Puropean defense. 

Today, not only has rearmament 
imposed a heavy direct burden but 
the global consequences of rear- 
mament—including rises in the 
prices both of raw materials gen- 
erally and of finished goods from 


vy |the United States—have drastica)-| 


ly upset the European balance of 
payments, Substantial and sus-

\margin of raw materiais amu, 
jother support for their defense 
efforts. If we provide this margin 
of resources, the European coun-' 
tries will be able to produce far, 
more military equipment than they 
otherwise could, and to maintain| 
far larger armed forces than would 
otherwise be possible. 

Our defense support will allow 
them to use plants, machinery, ma- 
terials and manpower which exist 
in Europe, but which otherwise 
could not be devoted to defense’ 
purposes. For this reason, our de- 
fense support is an extremely eco- 
nomical way to achieve military 
strength for our mutual security. 
The funds included in the Mutual 
Security program for defense sup- 
port will yield, according to the 
best estimates, more than twice as 
much military strength in Europe 
as would the same funds spent for 
the direct transfer of military 
equipment from the United States. 

Accordingly, the Mutual Secu- 
rity Program for Europe is 
planned so that the United States 
will provide both weapons and de- 
fense support. The form of assis- 
tance—whether military equip- 
ment or assistance in financing 
imports of raw materials and other! 
items where required to make. 
possible the necessary level of 
European defense efforts—has 
been decided in each case on the 
basis of which form produces the, 
most results in defensive strength 
at the least cost. 

In addition to the North At- 
lantic Treaty countries and West- 
jern Germany, limited amounts are 
included in the Mutual Security 

Program for Yugoslavia, whose 
defiance of the Soviet Union is 
giving heart to untold millions be- 
hind the Iron Curtain; for Austria, 
where continued economic assis- 
tance is necessary to maintain 
economic stability in the face of 
occupation of part of the country 
by Soviet forces; and for facilitat- 
ing emigration from Europe under 
international arrangements. 

We expect soon to complete ar- 
rangements with Spain which will 
assist in the defense of the Medi- 
terranean area; our part in these 
arrangements will be carried for- 
ward with funds already made 
available by the Congress. 


Asia, Africa, and Latin 
America 


building collective strength for 
peace must meet and overcome a 
lvery different range of problems. 
The most serious problems of Asia, 
Africa and Latin America occur 
in the underdeveloped areas—the 
lareas which have not yet shared in 
ithe benefits of the burst of scienti- 


fic and technical advance of the 


last two centuries. 


The people of many of these 


Outside of Europe, our policy of 


‘areas confront the legacy of c - 
Ties of neglect—they pend in 
‘cases desperately poor, defenseless 
before famine and disease, disabled 
by illiteracy. At the same time, | 
they have a new and burning de-, 
termination to improve their liv- 
ing standards, to fulfill their desire 
for self-government, to control 
their own futures. As old social 
structures have failed to meet the 
basic needs of their peoples, the 
popular energy, so long pent up, is 
bursting forth in fierce national- 


ism and in fierce demands for real 
‘economic change. 

‘| These conditions would exist 
‘leven if there were no Soviet threat 
to world peace. But the pressure 
of Soviet communism, working 
‘overtime to éxploit the turbulence 
the underdeveloped areas, 
greatly increases the necessity for 
‘speed in meeting these conditions 
—speed in the imterest, not alone 
‘of orderly and democratic develop- 
iment, but of the security of the 
\whole free world. 

' As a nation born in a struggle 
for individual freedom, we cordially 
‘welcome the aspirations of people 
‘to free themselves from oppression 


and misery. To place ourselves 


\whole-heartedly at their side, we 


‘must work with them in their 


struggle against poverty and fa- 
mine and illiteracy and disease. In 
the Point Four concept we have a 
means of joining hands with the 
constructive forces of these areas 
before bitterness and frustration 
drive them into a fatal alliance 
with Soviet communism. 


Meaning of Point Four 


Point Four means making our 
scientific advances and technical 
‘know-how available for the im- 
provement and growth of under- 
developed areas. Point Four means 
technical missionaries at work, and 
it also means the supplies and 
‘equipment that are needed to put 
new techniques into effect. 

No one should think that Point 
Four involves some single formula 
or program which is to be applied, 
everywhere, in equal measure, 
throughout the underdeveloped 
regions of the world. The kinds of, 
aid we plan must be tailored both 
to what we can afford at any given| 
time and to the specifie situation in 
each country, Our experience in 
Latin America has demonstrated 
that Point Four operations, to be 
successful, must be supported by 
adequate supplies and equipment. 
The supplies and equipment can be 
financed in various ways. 

Some countries can attract pri- 
vate investment capital and loans 
|to finance most of their outlays for 
economic development. Other coun- 
‘tries can earn enough dollats from 
their own exports to finance most 
of the equipment and supplies they 


In still other countries, where 
neither loans nor private capital 
can meet the need, this Govern- 
ment must provide substantial 


quantities of supplies and equip- 


ment to assure real progress on 
vital programs for development. 
That is the direction we are taking 
in India today, and in other places 
where the need is particularly 
lunges and where the local plans 
are firm enough to produce a sound 
result. 

Today, we have technical and 
economic missions in forty coun- 
‘tries. The shirtsleeve diplomats of 
Point Four are carrying the Amer- 
‘ican revolution to the villages and 
farms of the world. They are pro- 
\viding farmers with better seed 
and better fertilizer, better methods 
of plowing and sowing and better 
‘means of harvesting and saying 
the crops. 


Disease and Ignorance 


They are helping to fight malaria 
and dysentery, trachoma and 
rinderpest. They are providing 
training in the techniques of mod- 
ern government. They are helping 
o build roads and canals and dams, 
schools and hospitals. They are 


teaching people to read, to revital- 
ize the soil, to irrigate it, to drain 
it. In short, they are teaching peo- 
ple by methods of peace to change 
their own wotld without blood- 
shed. | 
The funds we invest in Point 
Four will yield direct and imme- 
diate results in terms of larger 
food production, better communi- 
cations, more agricultural and 
health specialists, engineers, and 
other technicians. But even more 
important are the longer term re- 
sults. 
_ For the magic of this work is 
its multiplying effect: If we can 
help train ten teachers, they can 
train hundreds of children; if we 
can help set up ten demonstration 
farms, hundreds of farmers can 
come and learn to u w meth- 
ods; if we can 
new wells or b ew irriga- 
tion dam, thousands of farmers 
can increase their yields and plow 
back their earnings into further 
improvements. In this way, a rela- 
tively small investment can bring 
immense results. 
In one district in India, the pro- 
duction of food has already been 
increased 46 per cent. Repeat this 
across the continents of Asia and 
Africa and Latin America, and we 
enter a new era in the history of 
man. 


The Near East and Africa 


The Near East presents a sharp 
challenge to American statesman- 
ship. The counrties of these areas 
are of vital importance to the se- 
curity of the free world, but the 
problems of achieving constructive 
and orderly development Are ex- 


tremely difficult. 
Living standards are generally 


very low. Transportation and land’ 


tenure systems are often archaic. 
Political and religious controver- 
sles simmer throughout the region. 
Nationalism is sometimes misdi- 
rected into fanatical outbursts 


which ignore the benefits to be 
gained from international coopera- 
tion. The Communists are doing 
their. best to stir up confusion and 
trouble. 

Most of these problems_can only 
|be solved by the people of these 
jcountries finding ways to make 
‘solid progress in developing eco- 
nomic strength and effective free 
institutions. But we can and must 
help them. 

We can help dig wells for irri- 
gation and clean water in Iran and 
Iraq. We can help set up farm 
credit institutions and agricultural 
extension services in Lebanon and 
Liberia. We can help build roads 
and establish public health services 
in Israel. We can help build up 
school ard hospital services in 
countries throughout the area for 
projects of this type. I recommend 
economic and technical assistance 
in this area (including help for the 
Arab refugees) of $196,000,000. 

Military assistance for nations in 
this area is recommended in the 
amount of $606,000,000. Most of 
these funds are for Greece and 
Turkey, whose military assistance 
programs are carried under the 
heading of the Near East; defense 
support funds for those countries 
are included with those for Europe. 

To help in maintaining security 
:|in the Near East, the United States 
‘has joined with Turkey, France, 
Great Britain, and three Common- 


wealth countajes in proposing the 
eaagire of a Middle East 
.,Com. ope this command

Asia and the Pacific 


Much of Asia at this moment is 
‘under Communist attack. The free 
nations are holding the line against 
‘aggression in Korea and Indo- 
‘China, and are -hattling Commu- 
nist-inspired disorders in Burma, 
‘Malaya, and the Philippines. The 
loss of any of these countries 
would mean the loss of freedom for 
millions of people, the loss of vital 
raw materials, the loss of points of 
critical strategic importance to the 
free world. 

The Mutual Security Program 
for this area includes military 
assistance in the amount of $611,- 
000,000, and economic and techni- 
cal assistance of $408,000,000, some 
of which will contribute directly. 
to the defense programs of certain. 
countries of Southeast Asia. 


— 


Of pur military assistance, a 
large part will go to Indo-China 
where the troops of the French 
Union and of the Associated States 
are battling valiantly against the 
Communist-led forces, and another 
large part will go to continue to 
‘help prepare the Chinese armies on 
Formosa to resist Communist ag- 
gression, The rest will go to the 
Philippines and Thailand, to help 
build forces strong enough to in- 
sure internal security. 

As in the Near East and Africa, 
however, security in Asia is far 
more than a military problem. Our 
military assistance is essential to 
check the encroachments of Com- 
munist imperialism, But the long- 
‘run promise of stability and prog- 
‘ress lies, not alone in arms, but in 
the provision of sufficient economic 
and technical support to enable the 
peoples of Asia to conquer their 
‘old, deep-seated and agonizing eco- 
nomic problems and to share in 
the benefits of an expanding world 
economy. 


The Problem in India 


In India, for example, the key 
to economic progress lies in boost- 
ing food production. This is the 
only way to remove the constant 
threat of famine and ease the 
‘desperate struggle for a daily 
livelihood. It is the only way of 
freeing funds now spent to im- 
port food, so they can be used in- 
stead for productive investment in 
developing natural resources, trans- 
portation, and industry. 

The whole future of India as a 
free nation may well lie in her 
ability to raise her food produc- 
tion and do it quickly. 

We must support India’s own ef- 
forts to get this done. The Indian 
Government has in 
motion a plan‘\u a 
very few years,, to 
grow the food heeded by her 
people, and will have established 
a sound basis for further economic 
development. It is a good plan, 
practical and definite. India itself 
is financing most of it. And we 
are greatly stepping up our aid for 
this plan with confidence that the 
sums we spend will bring concrete 
results. 

This is an example of how our 
aid can produce large-scale re 
‘by supporting the efforts of the 
people ofthe Asian countries. In 
‘the same way. we are helping to 
expand irrigation in Pakistan, to 
eliminate malaria in Thailand, to 
increase rice yields in Burma. 

It is vital that this work be car- 
ried forward rapidly. For in this 
region, there is still time to set inf 
motion programs which will tap 
the energies of the people and give 
‘them solid hope for advancement 
‘under Governments determined to 
resist Communist expansion. We 
must not let this opportunity go 
iby default. 


wet it never be said of the 
American people that our eyes are 
focused only on what might have 
been—that we grow concerned 
about the countries of Asia only 
after they have been lost to the 
enemy. The bold and wise invest- 
ment of American funds in this 
region in the next few years can 
make a vital difference to the fu- 
ture of freedom. 

Spcial note should be taken of 
the contribution that the new, free 
Japan can make to the growth of 
economic strength in Asia. A 
growing trade partnership of Ja- 
pan with Southeast and South 
Asia can benefit everyone con- 
cerned. Such a partnership in free 
Asia can result in a self-support- 
ing, expanding regional economy, 
free of permanent dependéetice on 
United States economic aid and 
free from the danger of satellite 
slavery under the Soviet orbit. — 


Latin America 


I do not need to restate here the 
inestimable importance of “Latin 
America. Its governments and its 
peoples are joined with us im the 
organization of American. states 
‘and the Rio Treaty to bolster the 
‘security of the free world. It is a 
most important source of vital 
raw materials; and it carries on 
with us a large and mutually ad- 
vantageous trade. In case of emer 


gency, its military forces can par- 
tially relieve ours of some of the 
important tasks connected with 
Hemisphere defense. 

In order to assist Hemisphere 
defense, I am recommending mili- 
tary assistance of $62,000,000 for 
the Latin American countries. In, 
addition, I recommend $23,000,000 
to carry forward the remarkable 
technical cooperation work now 
under way in nineteen Latin Amer- 
ican states to develop agriculture 
‘and natural resources; education, 
‘health, transportation and other 
fundamental services. This includes 
$1,000,000 for our share of the 
technical] cooperation work of the 
organization of American states. 
This assistance — supplemented as 
‘it is by substantial amounts of pri- 
vate loans and investments and 
et loans through the Export- 

mport Bank and the International 
Bank—has already helped materi- 
ally to raise living standards, speed 
economic development and reduce 
vulnerability to undemocratic 
movements of the extreme right or 
the extreme left. 

The policy of the good neighbor 
has been one of our most euccess- 
ful policies; we must ret falter in 
i loyalty to that policy today,

The major nationat wecurity pro- 
grams I am recommending for the 
fiscal year 1953, including the Mu- 
tual Security Program, total about 
$64,000,000,000. This request raises

jonce again the question whetner 
‘the American nation can afford so 
much money for national security. 
This is a serious question. It re- 
quires @ serious answer. 

Certainly the total security pro- 
gram—of which the Mutual Secu- 
rity Program is a relatively small 
part—is by any standard a large 
one. It has resulted in some un- 
avoidable dislocations and _ infla- 
tionary pressures. Yet, the burden 
jhas been carried with remarkably 
little strain. 

_ The fundamental reason for this 
is that our national production has 
been expanding rapidly, and will 
jcontinue to rise. Security expendi- 
| tures, measured in 1951 prices, rose 
jabout $18,000,000,000 from 1950 to 


|1951; but the increase in our na- 


tional output was even larger— 


| totaling about $26,000,000,000. 


During the next two years we 


‘|can continue to raise output by 


not less than 5 per cent annually, 
increasing the gross national prod- 
uct (at 1951 prices) to about 
$340,000,000,000 to $345,000,000,000 
in 1952 and to about $355,000,000,- 
000 to $360,000,000,000 in 1953, 
compared with $327,000,000,000 in 
1951 and $301,000,000,000 in 1950, 

If output rises at this rate, we 
will have increased our total an- 
nual production about one-fifth in 
ithree years. Even with the im- 
‘mense diversion to security pur- 
poses, production should be high 
enough, by the beginning of 1953, 
‘to permit total civilian consump- 
jtion and capital investment at 
least 50 per cent higher than dur- 
ing World War II. 

There will certainly be cutbacks 
in some things. Yet, even if auto- 
mobile production should drop to 
around 4,000,000 units this year, it 
must be remembered that this is 
only slightly less than the average 
production of 1948 and 1949. If 
housing should dip below 1,000,000 
units, it must be remembered that 
we have succeeded in producing 
more than 1,000,000 units per year 
in only three years of our history. 
And as we expand our output of 
vital materials such as steel and 
aluminum, we can again increase 
the output of such civilian items. 

All in all, our present security 
expenditures are clearly within our 
economic capacity. And as our 
basic productive strength continues 
to increase in the years ahead, we 
should be able to carry more easily 
the substantial security costs which 
may continue to be necessary. 


Matter of Alternatives 


Let us consider for a moment 
the costs of possible alternatives to 
our present policy. 

The alternative of premeditated 
and deliberate war is one which no 
democratic or God-fearing people 
can for a moment entertain. Even 
if we were insane enough to con- 
sidér it, however, it would obvious- 


ly entail expenditures immensely 
greater than our present ones, not 
to speak of the terrible waste and 
destruction of human life, property 
and natural resources. 

Another alternative—of con- 
tracting our cemmitments and re- 
treating to the Western Hemis- 
phere—has a momentary seduc- 
tiveness, because it would seem to 
relieve us of the contributions we 
are now making to collective de- 
fense. But, in fact, if we followed 
the policy of retreat, we would 
have to try to replace the contri- 
butions to our security which now 
come from the cooperation of our 
Allies. 

We could not replace some of 
those contributions at any cost; 
others only at very high cost, not 
just in money, resources and mili- 
‘tary manpower, but in the precious 


political and economic freedoms we} 


are mobilizing to defend. 

The policy of retreat would de- 
prive us of armed forces which, if 
called upon to fight for the de- 
fense of their own countries, would 
at the same time be fighting for 
the defense of ours. It would de- 


prive us of essential raw mate- 


-lrials. It would impose upon us a 


much higher level of mobilization 
than we have today. 

{ It would require a stringent and 
comprehensive system of allocas 
tion and rationing in order to huse 
jband our smaller resources. It 
would require us to become a gars 
rison state, and to inypose upon 
ourselves a system of centralized 
regimentation unlike anything we 
have ever known. 

In the end, when the enemy, en- 
couraged by our retreat, began to 
organize the rest of the world 
against us, we would face the pros- 
pect of bloody battle—and on our 
own shores. The ultimate costs of 
such a policy would be incalculable, 


Its adoption would be a mandate 
for national ‘suicide. 


Appeal for Full Amount 


,__I am asking the Congress for 
$7,900,000,000 for the Mutual Se- 
curity Program—an amount which 
will bring returns no other policy 
could hope to produce so eco 
nomically. 

I am deeply convinced, after 
studying the matter carefully, that 
if there is any question about this 
amount, it is not whether it is too 
large, but whether it is to small. 

These funds are needed, all of 
them, to pay for essential parts of 
the total undertaking to help free 
nations build adequate combined 
idefenses. If the military assistance 
funds are reduced, this will mean 
a corresponding reduction in the 
effective combat forces which can 
be created in Europe and Asia, and 


| 


(a serious disruption of the time- 
table for achieving adequate de- 
| fenses. 

| If the defense support funds are 
jreduced, it will mean that our 
partners in this endeavor will be 
‘unable to raise and train the 
‘scheduled forces or unable to exe 
\pand their own military produc- 
tion as planned. If economic and 
technical funds are reduced there 
will be a corresponding reduction 
in what we can do to help coun-, 
tries in Asia, the Near East, Af- 
rica and Latin America to strength- 
eri themselves, and a correspond- 
ingly greater danger of these 
areas falling to Communist ag- 
gression or subversion. 

I would not counsel the Congress 
to spend one dollar more than is 
necessary to support our policy of 
peace, But there is no economy 
more false than that which is 
summed up in the tragic phrase, 
“Too little and too late.” Such a 
policy risks the loss of our invest- 
ment as well as our objective. It 
would be foolish and dangerous to 
withhold a dollar now at the risk 
of expending, not just many times 
as many dollars, but human lives 
as well, a few years later. 

The question is frequently—and 
properly—asked: How long are we 
going to have to continue this type 
of program? I cannot—no one can 
—give an answer in terms of a 
specific month and year. But I can 
say that one of the central pur- 
Poses in everything we are doing 
under the Mutual Security Pro- 
gram is to build strength which 
will eliminate the need for agsist- 
ance from the United States. 

This is not a program for carry- 
ing the rest of the world on our 
backs. This is a program for 
ting the other free nations on their 
own feet, so they can move ahead 
without special help from us or 
anyone else. 

As the Mutual Security Program 
moves ahead—as larger military 
forces become equipped and trained, 
as economic strength continues to 
increase—we can expect the costs 
to the United States to decline, 
This is not only our own desire; 
it is also the natural hopes anda 
objective of the people of other 
countries. 
Free people do not relish depend- 
ence on other nations. They wish 
to achieve as fapidly as possible 
the economic health and vigor 
which will enable thém to sustain 
their own programs of defense and 
economic progress. The Mutual 
Security Program will hasten the 
day when this will become possible. 
History has thrust a fearful 
responsibility up the United 
States. Today, the survival of 
reedom and civilization on this 
earth may depend on the initiative 
and decisions taken in our own 


nation’s capital. The free peoples 
look to us for leadership. Leader- 


ship implies more than a recogni- 
tion of the problem. 

It implies also a capacity te 
work out a joint resolution with 
our partners, and to stay with it 
till the end; it implies resolution 
and fortitude. We have shown 
that we understand the threat, 
But some are doubtful whether we 
will stay the course until we 
achieve peace in a free world. 

I am not in doubt. I know that 
we shall succeed. It is perhaps 
true that our history has. been 
characterized by impatience, by a 
passion for quick results. It is 
equally true, however, that it has 
also been characterized by per- 


severance and determination—the 
perseverance of the pioneer, mak- 
ing his steadfast way into the un- 
known West; the determination of 
the farmer and worker, transform- 
ing a savage wilderness into the 
strongest and most productive na- 
tion known to history. 

Preseverance and determination, 
steadfastness and dependability— 
it was these qualities, and not 
recklessness or impudence, which 
built America, It is our obligation 
to turn these qualities outward, 
We must show the world that we 
can meet any crisis, and that tem- 
porary frustration will not drive us 
to panicky aggression or to igno- 
minious retreat. This is the chal- 
lenge of free world leadership. 

In the last analysis, our leader- 
ship must stand or fall on the 
moral power behind it. No nation, 
of course, can undertake policies 
which are not squarely and solidly 
based on national self-interest. But 
world leadership in these perilous 
times calls for policies which, while 

ging from self-interest, tran- 


\‘sterd it-—policies which serve as 
a bridge between our own national 


objectives and the needs and as- 
pirations of other free people. 

I deeply believe that the Mutual 
Security Program is an expression 
of a new spirit in the world—a 
spirit based on faith in democracy 
and human decency, and looking 
to a new collaboration among na- 
tions and peoples. It expresses the 
deep reality of our friendship for 
other peoples—the sincerity of our 
determination to join with them in 
building »° world where freedom, 
justice and security will exist for 
all. HARRY S. TRUMAN, 

The White House, 

March 6, 1952.

THE WORLD FEDERATION OF TRADE UNIONS, AN ALL-PURPOSE 

REVOLUTIONARY ARM OF MOSCOW, HAS MADE IT CLEAR. 

BUT THERE ARE SECRET PLANS. TOO, FOR TYING THE DRIVE IN THIS 
COUNTRY TO THE WORLD REVOLUTION STALIN SEEKS. THE WFTU KEEPS QUIET 
ABOUT THOSE PLANS, BUT THERE IS NO DOUBT REMAINING THAT THEY 
CALL FOR CREATING CHAOS. IF AND WHEN MOSCOW SEES THE CHANCE. 

AS IN OTHER COUNTRIES, THE WFTU HAS ITS SPECIFIC PROGRAM FOR 
WEST GERMANY, MESHED WITH THE OVERALL EUROPEAN AND WORLD PLANS. 

THE DRIVE’IN GERMANY, AS ELSEWHERE IN EUROPE, IS AIMED AT THE 
STRATEGIC INDUSTRIES. SOME COMPETENT OBSERVERS HERE EXPRESS CONCERN 
AT THE INROADS IT APPEARS TO BE MAKING. 

ATTEMPTS AT INFILTRATION HAVE BEEN CONSIDERABLY STEPPED UP IN 
THE INDUSTRIAL RUHR VALLEY, WHERE THE COMMUNISTS HAVE BUILT UP A 
STRONG PARTY ORGANIZATION. SEMI-OFFICIAL SOURCES PLACE THE COMMUNIST 
PARTY STRENGTH IN WESTERN GERMANY AT 375,000 MEMBERS, OF WHOM FULLY 
150.000 ARE IN THE STRATEGIC RUHR. 

COMMUNIST STRENGTH WITHIN THE WEST GERMAN TRADE UNIONS HAD BEEN 
FALLING OFF STEADILY, ALONG WITH COMMUNIST OVERALL VOTING STRENGTH 
IN WEST GERMANY, UNTIL ABOUT MID-1951. NOW, HOWEVER, WITH THE 
CONCERTED RED CAMPAIGN KEYED TO THE REARMAMENT ISSUE, RED STRENGTH 
WAS BEEN MAKING SOME GAINS IN UNION RANKS. THIS IS CONFIRMED BY 
PERSONS IN A POSITION TO KNOW. 

SUST HOW MUCH THE COMMUNISTS HAVE GAINED IS KNOWN ONLY TO THE 
PARTY ITSELF. COMMUNIST HEADQUARTERS KEEPS TO ITSELF THE FIGURES 
ON ITS STRENGTH WITHIN THE UNIONS, AND WESTERN ALLIED SOURCES DECLINE 
TO ESTIMATE IT AT THE PRESENT TIME.

"I AT ONCE GAVE HIM YOUR NAME," LATTIMORE WROTE. 

LATTIMORE IS A TRUSTEE OF THE INSTITUTE OF PACIFIC AFFAIRS, WHICH 
FIGURES PROMINENTLY IN THE INQUIRY, AND ONCE WAS EDITOR OF ITS QUARTER- 
LY "PACIFIC AFFAIRS." FIELD ONCE WAS SECRETARY OF THE AMERICAN COUNCIL 
OF IPR, WHICH HAD COUNCILS IN VARIOUS COUNTRIES, INCLUDING RUSSIA. 

SENATOR FERGUSON (R-MICH) WANTED TO KNOW WHETHER LATTIMORE AT THAT 
TIME REGARDED FIELD AS A COMMUNIST. LATTIMORE SAID HE DIDN'T. 

FERGUSON CITED EARLIER LATTIMORE TESTIMONY WHICH, HE SAID INDICATED 
LATTIMORE REGARDED FIELD AS HAVING "VIGOROUS COMMUNIST SYMPATHIES" AS 


FARLY AS 1939, 
SEN. MCCARAN (D-NEV) REMINDED LATTIMORE THAT ALL OF HIS TESTIMONY 


HAD BEEN GIVEN UNDER OATH. | 

LATTIMORE REPLIED THAT UNDER THE PRESSURE OF CROSS-QUESTIONING HE 
HAD BECOME FATIGUED AND MAY HAVE BECOME CONFUSED IN HIS RECOLLECTION. 

MCCARRAN ASKED WHETHER LATTIMORE NOW REGARDS FIELD AS A COMMUNIST. 

"Y BELIEVE THAT HE PROBABLY IS," LATTIMORE SAID. “I HAVE NO DOUBT 
THAT HE BECAME ONE IN THE 1940'S, | 

THE LATE BRIG, GEN. EVANS Fe CARLSON. OF THE MARINES FIGURED BRIEFLY 
IN THE QUESTIONING. LATTIMORE SAID HE FIRST MET CARLSON IN CHINA YEARS 
AGO AT A TIME CARLSON WAS CONSIDERING RESIGNING FROM THE MARINES. LAT- 
TIMORE SAID HE URGED CARLSON NOT TO RESIGN BECAUSE, AS AN EXPERT ON 
CHINA, HE WAS USEFUL TO THE NATION. 

ROBERT MORRIS, A COMMITTEE LAWYER, SAID CARLSON HAS SERVED AS CHAIR- 
MAN OF THE COMMITTEE FOR A DEMOCRATIC FAR EAST, AND HAD BEEN IDENTI- 
FIED IN TESTIMONY AS A MEMBER OF THE COMMUNIST PARTY. 

LATTIMORE SAID HE DIDN'T KNOW WHETHER THE COMMITTEE WAS A COMMUNIST- 
FRONT, BUT "IT CERTAINLY HAS BECOME A FELLOW TRAVELER."

ARCH 8-(AP)-MOSCOW NEWSPAPERS ARE PUBLISHING MANY 
DEM NCIATIONS OF THE UNITED STATES 
FOR NOT RATIFYING A GENEVA CONVENTION BARRING BACTERIOLOGICAL WARFARE. 
(THERE IS NO GENEVA CONVENTION ON BACTERIOLOGICAL WARFARE. THE 
|UeS. HAS SIGNED OTHER GENEVA CONVENTIONS SEEKING TO LIMIT THE HORRORS 
OF WAR. THE U.sS. DID NOT SIGN ONE OF THE CONVENTIONS WHICH 
ATTEMPTED TO BAR CHEMICAL WARFARE ON THE GROUNDS ITS FORCES WOULD 
HAVE TO BE FREE TO RETALIATE IN KIND IF ANY ENEMY SHOULD RESORT TO 
SUCH WARFARE. HOWEVER, NO MENTION OF BACTERIOLOGICAL OR GERM WARFARE 
WAS MADE IN THAT CONVENTION OR ANY OTHER.) 
YURI DIKOV, STALIN PRIZE WINNER, SAID IN A LETTER PUBLISHED IN 
TRUD, TRADE UNION NEWSPAPER? 
"THE SOVIET PEOPLE DEMAND THE CESSATION OF THE SENSELESS 
BLOODSHED (IN KOREA). THERE MUST BE PEACE IN KOREA. THE HAND OF THE 
MURDERERS MUST BE STAYED," 
THE NEWSPAPERS THEMSELVES AND THEIR LETTERS TO THE EDITOR MORE AND 
M MORE ARE DEMANDING PEACE IN THE KOREAN WAR. THE U.S. IS GENERALLY 
Mm &lt;PICTURED AS NOT WANTING PEACE AND AS WANTING TO USE THE KOREAN 
\SCONFLICT TO SPREAD WAR TO CHINA AND THUS START A THIRD WORLD WAR. 
THE COMMENTATORS EMPHASIZE A CONTENTION THAT THIS IS NOT THE WISH 
§ OF THE AMERICAN PEOPLE BUT OF THEIR LEADERS AND MILITARISTS« 
“" THE MOSCOW PRESS SHOWED CONSIDERABLE CONCERN OVER CLAIMS BY 
COMMUNIST CHINA THAT U.S. PLANES HAD CARRIED BACTERIOLOGICAL WARFARE

SAN FRANCISCO, MARCH 10-(AP)-RED PILOTS OF THE RUSSIAN-BUILT MIG-15 
JETS FLYING OVER’ KOREA KILL A DOWNED MATE RATHER-IMAN ALLOW HIM TO 
FALL INTO ALLIED HANDS, AN AVIATION EXECUTIVE SAID TODAY ON HIS RETURN 
FROM A MONTH'S TOUR OF AIR FORCE BASES IN JAPAN AND KOREA. 

W. HOWARD EHMANN, DIRECTOR OF FIELD SERVICE FOR REPUBLIC AVIATION 
CORPORATION, MAKERS’ OF THE THUNDERJET (F84), SAID SOON AFTER HE ARRIVED 
IN KOREA AIR FORCE OFFICERS TOLD HIM OF THIS INSTANCE: 

A MIG WAS DAMAGED AND HAD TO MAKE A FORCED LANDING. ALLIED 
FIGHTERS CIRCLED THE AREA AND CALLED FOR A HELICOPTER TO COME AND 
BRING OUT THE MIG PILOT. BEFORE THE HELICOPTER COULD ARRIVE. MIGS 
TORE THROUGH THE ALLIED FIGHTERS AND MACHINEGUNNED THE GROUNDED FLIER.

7 THIS WAS THE BOX SCORE OF ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF THE THUNDERGET: |

DESTROYED OR DAMAGED, 20,000. LOCOMOTIVES AND RAILROAD CARS 
DESTROYED 2,250. BRIDGES AND TUNNELS WRECKED, 175.

COMMUNIST COMMUNICATIONS AND IT OPERATED UNDER COVER OF SABRE 
JETS. HE SAID, HOWEVER, THAT THE F84S SHOT DOWN 12 COMMUNIST PLANES,

(ADVANCE) WASHINGTON, MARCH 11-CAP)-GEN.DOUGLAS MACARTHUR IS QUOTED 
AS SAYING THERE IS LITTLE CHANCE RUSSIA WILL BE DISLODGED FROM THE 
KURILE ISLANDS AND THE SOUTHERN HALF OF SAKHALIN ISLAND NORTH OF 

SEN. O'CONOR (D-MD) REPORTED THIS TODAY ON THE BASIS OF A LETTER 
HE RECEIVED FROM MACARTHUR ABOUT THE JAPANESE PEACE TREATY. | 

O'CONOR HAD ASKED THE GENERAL FOR HIS VIEWS ON SEVERAL POINTS CON- 
CERNING THE TREATY, WHICH NOW IS BEFORE THE SENATE FOR RATIFICATION. 
DEBATE ON IT STARTS NEXT MONDAY. 

THE SENATOR SAID MACARTHUR WROTE HIM THAT RUSSIA NOW IS IN POSSES- 
SION OF THE KURILES AND THE SOUTHERN HALF OF SAKHALIN, AND THAT HE SEES 
LITTLE LIKELIHOOD THE SOVIETS WOULD GIVE THEM UP. : 

THE GENERAL SAID "IT WOULD PROBABLY TAKE MILITARY FORCE TO DISLODGE 
THEIR CONTROL." AND HE EXPRESSED DOUBT THAT ANY SUCH EFFORT HAS BEEN 
GIVEN OR WOULD RECEIVE SERIOUS CONSIDERATION, O'CONOR SAID. 

THE WORLD WAR II ALLIES AGREED AT YALTA THAT THE KURILES AND THE 
SOUTHERN HALF OF SAKHALIN WOULD GO TO RUSSIA AFTER THE VICTORY. 

i HOWEVER» THE JAPANESE TREATY--WHICH RUSSIA DID NOT SIGN--IS SILENT 
‘THE FOREIGN RELATIONS COMMITTEE SAID IN A RESOLUTION APPROVING THE 
TREATY THAT THE PACT WAS NOT TO BE CONSIDERED A CONFIRMATION OF RUS- 

SIA'S RIGHT TO THE ISLANDS. 

THERE WAS TESTIMONY BEFORE THE COMMITTEE THESE ISLANDS WOULD BE 
STRATEGICALLY VALUABLE TO RUSSIA FOR SUBMARINE BASES AND OTHER PUR- 
POSES, AND ALSO WOULD POSE A THREAT TO JAPAN. 

O'CONOR REPORTED MACARTHUR ADVISED HIM THAT HE FELT JAPAN ITSELF 
WOULD HAVE TO DECIDE WHAT DIPLOMATIC RELATIONSHIPS IT WOULD ENTER INTO

RUSSIAN REVOLUTION, WILL BE TRANSMITTED BY THE VOICE OF AMERICA. 

ITS SPONSORS SAID tT WOULD BE CARRIED ALSO BY RADIO FREE EUROPE 
AND "OTHER INFORMATION MEDIA."

HERBERT HOOVER, A NUMBER OF REPUBLICAN AND DEMOCRAT SENATORS, 
INDUSTRIALISTS, UNION LEADERS AND EDUCATORS.

HINTED AT THE POSSIBILITY OF OVERTHROWING. COMMUNISM.

ASSUME HER NORMAL PLACE IN THE INTERNATLONAL COMMUNITY..."

"AMERICANS WHO CHERISH THEIR OWN FREEDOM REALIZE TODAY THAT A

ASSURANCE AGAINST A DEVASTATING WORLD WAR."

WASHINGTON, MARCH 12=(AP)-THE FATHERS OF TWO AMERICAN DEAD TODAY 
RECEIVED THE MEDALS OF HONOR WON BY THEIR SOLDIER SONS ON KOREAN BATTLE- 

SECRETARY OF THE ARMY PACE PRESENTED THE NATION'S HIGHEST MILITARY 
HONORS TO VAN CHARLTON, FATHER 'OF SGT. CORNELIUS H.«CHARLTON, AND JOSEPH 
SUDUT, FATHER OF 2ND Lt. JEROME A.SUDUT. 

THE MEDALS WERE GIVEN TO THE TWO FATHERS IN THE PRESENCE OF THE 

BY SACRIFIC LIVES IN ONE- 
i FA! Q THE CEREMONY FROM THEIR HOME AT 617 
WEST 147TH STs, THE BRONX, NEW YORK CITY. MR. AND MRS. SUDUT AND A 
SISTER, MISS DIANA SUDUT,’ CAME FROM WAUSAU, WIS, 

SGT. CHARLTON, THE SECOND NEGRO TO WIN THE MEDAL OF HONOR IN KOREA, 
TOOK COMMAND OF A PLATOON OF THE 25TH DIVISION WHEN ITS LIEUTENANT 
WAS WOUNDED IN A BITTER ATTACK, CHARLTON WAS THRICE WOUNDED HIMSELF, 

| | OCK OUT AN ENEMY STRON 
NDED BEFORE THE LAST CHARGE AND WAS 
BLEEDING PROFUSELY. STILL, HE MANAGED TO SILENCE THE COMMUNIST GUNS 
AND GRENADES WHICH HAD TAKEN A HEAVY TOLL AMONG HIS MEN. 

LT. SUDUT'S HEROISM ACHIEVED WHAT AMERICAN ARTILLERY, TANK AND 
MORTOR FIRE HAD FAILED TO DO. HE COMMANDED A PLATOON OF THE 27TH 
REGIMENT OF THE 25TH DIVISION WHICH HAD BEEN PINNED DOWN BY FURIOUS 
CROSS FIRE FROM SEVERAL ENEMY BUNKERS. TWICE HE MOVED UP A HILL 
THROUGH THIS FIRE, USING HIS PISTOL AND THROWING GRENADES AT THE 
ENTRENCHED REDS. HE WAS TWICE WOUNDED BUT REFUSED MEDICAL AID AND A 
THIRD TIME CHARGED ALONE UP THE SLOPE. WHEN HIS AMMUNITION WAS EX- 
HAUSTED HE USED HIS TRENCH KNIFE WITH SUCH DEVASTATING EFFECT ZHAT HIS 
MEN WERE ABLE TO SWEEP OVER THE CREST OF THE HILL AND SECURE THE: 
POSITION WHICH HAD HELD UP THE AMERICAN ADVANCE FOR HOURS, — » 


SGT. CHARLTON WAS BORN IN EAST GULF, We VA., IN 1929. HE ENTERED 
THE ARMY IN 1946, WENT TO KOREA IN OCTQBER, 1930 AND WAS KILLED L 
JUNE. HIS FATHER IS AN UNEMPLOYED PORTER iN THE BRONX. ory 


LT. SUDUT WON HIS COMMISSION ON THE FIELD OF BATTLE, TWO MONTHS 
BEFORE HE LOST_HIS LIFE LAST JULY. HE ENLISTED IN THE ARMY IN 1946, 
SERVED IN THE FAR EAST FOR THREE YEARS BEFORE THE KOREAN WAR AND 


RETURNED THERE FOR HIS FINAL TOUR OF DUTY ONE MONTH AF \ 
STARTED IN 1950. AFTER THE CONFLICT

OF SABOTAGE WAS DESCRIBED TODAY BY UNDERCOVER AGENT DANIEL “SCARLETTO AT 


THE FEDERAL CONSPIRACY TRIAL OF 15 CALIFORNIA PARTY LDADERS. 

SCARLETTO TESTIFIED ON CROSS-EXAMINATION THAT THE CHAIRMAN OF HIS 
CLUB ADVISED MEMBERS TO HAVE THEIR RELATIVES "GET INTO THE ARMY SO WE 
CAN SET UP PLANS LIKE THE RUSSIANS DID IN THEIR REVOLUTION." 

SCARLETTO. WHO WAS ACTING AS AN UNDERCOVER MAN FOR THE FBI, SAID 
MEMBERS OF THE CLUB CHEERED WHEN "I SAID THAT I COULD KEEP A LOT OF 
PLANES ON THE GROUND." 

HE EXPLAINED HE WAS AN AIRCRAFT MECHANIC IN THE NAVY AND ALSO AT. 
LOCKHEED AIRCRAFT CORP. LATER. 
CHIEF DEFENSE ATTORNEY BEN MARGOLIS’ THEN ASKED HIM3 "DO YOU KNOW OF

PARTY GETS TO LAY A HAND ON AN A NE. |

GERTRUDE STOUGHTON=-ASKED HIM TO POINT OUT ON A MAP U.S AIR BASES IN 
THE SOUTH PACIFIC, WHERE HE HAD SERVED. SCARLETTO INDICATED HE VENT 
THROUGH THE MOTIONS. 

BOTH MEETINGS WERE HELD IN 1950, THE WITNESS SAID. HE DID NOT LINK 
ANY OF THE DEFENDANTS TO THESE MEETINGS. 

SCARLETTO LATER QUOTED DEFENDANT BEN DOBBS AS URGING IN A 1950 SPEECH 
THAT PARTY MEMBERS ACT QUICKLY TO CIRCULATE STOCKHOLM PEACE PETITIONS 
"DFFORE THE FBI COULD KILL" THE PROGRAM. HE SAID THAT DOBBS ALSO 

ENTIONED, APPARENTLY APPROVINGLY, COMMUNIST SABOTAGING OF AMERICAN 
ROCKET LAUNCHERS AT NICE, FRANCE. 

DEFENSE ATTORNEYS TRIED TO DISCREDIT SCARLETTO'S TESTIMONY WITH 

QUESTIONS ABOUT COMMUNIST THEORIES AND DISCUSSIONS. 


THE YOUNG UNDERCOVER MAN GENERALLY ANSWERED THAT_HE DIDN'T REMEMBER, 
OR INDICATED HE WASN'T INTERESTED IN THE PARTY'S THEORIES.

IN ASIA,” AND BOOKS BY EDGAR SNOW AND ISRAEL EPSTEIN. 

BAS ICALLY MATUSOW SAID, THE LATTIMORE-SNOW-EPSTEIN VOLUMES WERE 
"THE BOOKS THE PARTY STATED CARRIED .THE PARTY LINE ON CHINA." 


MATUSOW TESTIFIED NE JOINED THE COMMUNIST PARTY IN 1947, BECAME 

DISILLUSIONED IN 1950, OFFERED HIS SERVICES TO THE FBI AND SERVED IT AS 
N INFORMER FOR ABOUT'A YEAR. HE SAID HE NOW LIVES IN AKRON, OHIO, 

AND WORKS ON THE STAFF OF THE OHIO UNAMERICAN ACTIVITIES COMMISSION. 

LATTIMORE IS A JOHNS HOPKINS UNIVERSITY PROFESSOR WHO SERVED FROM 
TIME TO TIME AS A STATE DEPARTMENT CONSULTANT ON FAR EASTERN AFFAIRS 
DURING THE LAST WAR. 

HE RECENTLY SPENT 10 STORMY DAYS BEFORE THE SENATE GROUP DURING 

HE 


WHICH HE DENIED HE WAS A COMMUNIST OR THAT HIS BOOK FOLLOWE 
COMMUNIST LINE. 7 

WHEN HE WAS WORKING IN RED BOOKSHOPS IN NEW YORK, MATUSOW TOLD THE 
SENATORS, HE CONSIDERED LATTIMORE, SNOW AND EPSTEIN COMMUNISTS. 

SNOW BENIED PREVIOUS TESTIMONY BY LOUIS BUDENZ THAT HE WAS A 
COMMUNIST AND CHALLENGED HIM TO MAKE THE CHARGE OUTSIDE CONGRESS, 
WHERE HE COULD BE SUED. 

SENATOR FERGUSON (R=MICH) SUGGESTED THAT EVERY ONE WHOSE BOOK WAS 
SOLD IN A COMMUNIST BOOKSHOP WAS NOT NECESSARILY A COMMUNIST. 

"THAT'S RIGHT," THE MATUSOW SAID. 

FERGUSON THEN ASKED HIM WHAT HE MEANT BY SAYING THAT HE REGARDED: 
LATTIMORE AND SNOW, A PROLIFIC WRITER ON ASIAN AFFAIRS, AS COMMUNISTS. 
"ON THEIR THINKING, THEIR IDEOLOGY," MATUSOW REPLIED. HE SAID HE 

FELT THEY AGREED WITH’"THE PRINCIPLE OF DIALECTICAL MATERIALISM." 

LATTIMORE IS A TRUSTEE OF THE INSTITUTE OF PACIFIC RELATIONS, AND 
WALLACE'S PAMPHLET WAS PUBLISHED BY THE IPR. 

THE SENATORS ARE INVESTIGATING THE INSTITUTE IN SEARCH OF ANY SUB- 
VERSIVE INFLUENCES WHICH MIGHT HAVE AFFECTED AMERICAN POLICY IN THE 
FAR EAST AFTER THE WAR.

TEHRAN. IRAN, MARCH 16-(AP)-THE WORLD BANKS ATTEMPT TO GET IRANIAN 
OIL FLOWING AGAIN TO THE WEST BROKE DOWN TONIGHT IN A_DEADLOCK WITH THE 
IRANLAN GOVERNMENT. 

A BANK MISSION, HEADED BY HECTOR PRUDYONME, LOAN OFFICER, WILL PAY 
A FAREWELL CALL ON PREMIER MOHAMMED EGH TOMORROW MORNING 
AND RETURN LATER THIS WEEK TO THE UNITED STATES. 

IN A BROADCAST OVER THE TEHRAN RADIO TONIGHT, ALI SHAYEGAN, A MEMBER 
OF IRAN'S JOINT OIL BOARD, SAID: "NEGOTIATIONS ARE NoW ENDED. 

SHAYEGAN SAID THE GOVERNMENT AND THE BANK HAD FAILED TO AGREE ON THE 
USE OF BRITISH TECHNICIANS, THE BANK'S POSITION IN OPERATING THE 
INDUSTRY, AND THE PRICE FOR THE OIL. MOSSADEGH HAS REFUSED TO PERMIT ANY 
OF THE OUSTED BRITISH TECHNICIANS OF THE BRITISH-CONTROLLED ANGLO~ 
IRANIAN OIL CO.(AIOC), WHOSE PROPERTIES IN IRAN WERE NATIONALIZED 
LAST YEAR, TO RETURN TO THIS COUNTRY» ON THE OTHER HAND, THE BANK 
HAS BEEN fNSISTING IT COULD NOT DISCRIMINATE AGAINST TECHNICIANS 
FROM ANY OF ITS 50 MEMBER COUNTRIES. 

OTHER RELIABLE SOURCES LISTED THE DEADLOCK POINTS AS: THE PRICE 
FOR WHICH THE BANK WOULD SELL CRUDE OIL AND REFINED PRODUCTS TO AIOC, 
THE USE OF BRITISH TECHNICIANS, AND THE PERCENTAGE AND PRICE OF OIL 
WHICH IRAN WOULD BE PERMITTED to SELL ON THE WORLD MARKET INDEPENDENTLY 

SHAYEGAN DECLARED THAT "IT IS THE DUTY OF THE IRANIAN GOVERNMENT TO 
IGNORE THE LOSS OF OIL INCOME" AND SET ITS PRESENT GOVERNMENTAL 


FINANCES IN ORDER. ; 
THE LOSS OF OIL REVENUES, A MAJOR SOURCE OF INCOME FOR THIS COUNTRY, 
ALREADY HAS FORCED THE COUNTRY TO MAKE DRASTIC ECONOMIES. 

THE BANK'S MISSION WAS THE FOURTH ATTEMPT TO SOLVE THE PROBLEM OF 
IRAN'S STALLED OIL INDUSTRY. A PREVIOUS ATTEMPT WAS MADE BY We 
AVERELL HARRIMAN. PRESIDENT TRUMAN'S FOREIGN ADVISER AND NOW HEAD OF 
THE UsS MUTUAL SECURITY ADMINISTRATION, TO BRING ABOUT AGREEMENT BETWEE 

IN ITS TRY. THE BANK PROPOSED TO RUN THE NATIONALIZED INDUSTRY FOR 
TWO YEARS OR LESS« HOPING THAT IRAN AND BRITAIN IN THE MEANTIME WOULD 
WORK OUT A PERMANENT ARRANGEMENT. 

IN HIS BROADCAST. SHAYEGAN SAID IRAN HAD WANTED THE BANK TO ACT AS 
HER AGENT BUT THAT THE BANK TOOK THE POSITION IT WAS INTERVENING 
IN A DISPUTE BETWEEN TWO OF ITS MEMBER NATIONS=--BRITAIN AND IRAN-=AND 
WANTED TO OPERATE THE INDUSTRY INDEPENDENTLY. SHAYEGAN SAID IRAN HAD 
TURNED DOWN THIS PROPOSAL BECAUSE IT WOULD BE AN ADMISSION OF THE 
RIGHT OF AIOC TO OPERATE IN IRAN. 


A85 

AN INFORMED SOURCE SAID AGREEMENT COULD NOT BE REACHED IN THE 
NEGOTIATIONS ON HOW MUCH OIL IRAN COULD SELL INDEPENDENTLYe THE PRAC@ 
TICE IN THIS AREA IS FOR THE PRODUCING COUNTRY TO SELL ONE-EIGHTH OF 
ITS OUTPUT ON THE WORLD MARKET PROVIDED IT SELLS FOR ABOVE THE POSTED 


IRAN REPORTEDLY INSISTED THAT SHE BE PERMITTED. TO SELL 30 PER CENT 
OF HER OIL INDEPENDENTLY AND AT ANY PRICE SHE MIGHT CHOOSE, AIOC 
APPARENTLY FEARED THAT IRAN WOULD CUT PRICES TO BUILD UP HER OWN 
MARKETS. IT WAS UNDERSTOOD THAT AIOC WOULD AGREE ONLY FOR IRAN TO SELL 
ONE-EIGHTH OF HER OUTPUT AT THE POSTED PRICE. 

THE IRANIAN PARLIAMENT VOTED A YEAR AGO YESTERDAY TO NATIONALIZE OIL 
WITH THE STORAGE TANKS BRIMMING FULL, THE NATIONALIZED REFINERIES WERE 


VIRTUALLY IDLE BY LAST DECEMBER.

THE COMMUNISTS IN KOREA WILLUINVITE MILITARY DISASTER IF THEY TURN 
FROM STALLING IN THE TRUCE NEGOTIATIONS TO GAMBLE ON A NEW OFFENSIVE. 

PENTAGON OBSERVERS RECENTLY RETURNED FROM INSPECTION OF THE BATTLE 
FRONT HINTED TODAY OF THE POWERFUL DEFENSIVE PREPARATIONS MADE BY 
UNITED NATIONS FORCES=&lt;-OF A SHARP BUILDUP IN FIREPOWER OF ALL TYPES 4 
OF MASSED ARTILLERY AND OTHER WEAPONS, OF AMPLE STOCKS OF AMMUNITIO 

THEY COMMENTED IN INTERVIEWS ON AN AIR OF CONFIDENCE DISPLAYED BY 
BOTH TROOPS AND TROOP COMMANDERS, BORDERING ALMOST ON A HOPE THAT THE 
ENENY WOULD TRY AN OFFENSIVE AND’ OPEN HIMSELF TO EXPECTED 

THIS GAVE EMPHASIS TO A STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF DEFENSE LOVETT 
OVER THE WEEKEND. MADE IN HIS SEMI-ANNUAL REPORT TO THE WHITE HOUSE 
AND CONGRESS, THA 
ED IN KOREA AND THAT "ANY RESUMPTION OF THE OFFENSIVE BY THE ENEMY 
WILL INVOLVE HIM IN CRITICAL LOSSES OF MEN AND MATERIEL." 

ON THE BASIS OF MILITARY EVIDENCE, THE INTENTIONS OF THE CHINESE AND 
NORTH KOREAN COMMUNISTS ARE NOT CLEAR. FOR MONTHS THEY HAVE BEEN 
PREPARING FOR BOTH OFFENSIVE AND DEFENSIVE OPERATIONS, WHILE HIGHER 
POLITICAL LEVELS OF THE COMMUNIST WORLD HAVE DIRECTED THE STALEMATES 

N TRUCE TALKS.

ANNOUNCED LAST WEEK THAT RUSSIA HAS BEEN EQUIPPING BOTH CHINESE AND 
KOREAN COMMUNIST FORCES WITH “A WIDE VARIETY OF ARMS. 

AMONG THEM ARE WEAPONS OF OBVIOUS OFFENSIVE NATURE, INCLUDING TANKS, 
MECHANIZED FIELD GUNS AND LONG RANGE ARTILLERY. ON THE OTHER HAND

THE ARMY ANNOUNCED LAST AUGUST THAT PRIMAQUINE WAS BEING TESTED 
EXTENSIVELY IN THE FIELD AND MIGHT PROVIDE A RAPID CURE FOR MALARIA. 
MALARIA HAS BEEN COMBATTED AMONG U.S. TROOPS IN KOREA BY DOSAGES OF

THE DRUG ATABRINE USED IN WORLD WAR Ii, 


IS NEITHER A COMPLETE PREVEN=- 
TATIVE NOR A COMPLETE CURE FOR MALARIA. 


THE ARMY SAYS IT HAS FOUND THAT PRIMAQUINE IS PARTICULARLY EFFECTIVE 
AGAINST THE PHASE OF MALARIA WHEN IT APPEARS IN THE LIVER CELLS. THIS 
FINDING HAS LED TO THE USE OF BOTH CHLOROQUINE AND PRIMAQUINE FOR 
ALL TROOPS RETURNING FROM KOREA BY SURFACE SHIP SINCE LAST DECEMBER. 
THE THE TREATMENT TAKES 14 CONSECUTIVE DAYS, SO MEN RETURNING BY AIR 
HAVE NOT ALL BEEN GIVEN THE TREATMENT. a 

THE ARMY WANTS TO GET THE NEW TESTS UNDERWAY BEFORE * ‘&lt; 
SUMMER, BECAUSE MALARIA, IF IT RECURS AT ALL, GENERALLY BREAKS OUT DUR- 
ING WARM WEATHER.

PEACE TREATY. IT MAY BE PUT TO MOSCOW BY THE END OF THIS WEEK. 

THE INFORMANTS SAID THE UNITED STATES, BRITAIN AND FRANCE HELD 
NO GREAT HOPE FOR A CLEAR AFFIRMATIVE ANSWER FROM MOSCOW. 

IF MOSCOW'S ANSWER IS NEGATIVE OR HEDGED ABOUT WITH CRIPPLING 
QUALIFICATIONS. THE WEST WILL REGARD THE RUSSIAN IDEAS AS JUST 
ANOTHER PROPAGANDA MOVE. 

THE SOVIET PROPOSALS, MADE MARCH 10 IN NOTES TO THE THREE WESTERN 
NATIONS, WERE BEING SUBJECTED TO INTENSIVE STUDY IN WASHINGTON, PARIS 
AND BONN. AS WELL AS HERE. THE TASK OF DRAFTING THE WEST'S REPLY 
WAS PROCEEDING AT A RAPID PACE IN LONDON. 

THE RUSSIANS PROPOSED THAT FOUR-POWER TALKS BE HELD WITHOUT | 
DELAY, AND THAT A PEACE TREATY BE WORKED OUT WITH THE DIRECT 
PARTICIPATION OF AN ALL-GERMANY GOVERNMENT. THEY ALSO SUGGESTED 
THAT THE TREATY PROVIDE FOR THE UNIFICATION AND LIMITED REMILITARIZATION 
OF GERMANY. ON CONDITION THAT SHE REMAIN OUTSIDE THE WESTERN- 

SPONSORED NORTH ATLANTIC DEFENSE SETUP. THE RUSSIANS DUCKED THE 
ELECTION QUESTION.

THE PROSPECTS ARE FOR GENUINELY FREE, NATIONWIDE GERMAN ELECTIONS 
ARRIVED AT BONN YESTERDAY TO BEGIN ITS STUDIES. IT HAS BEEN WELCOMED 
BY THE WESTERN HIGH COMMISSIONERS AND BY WEST GERMAN CHANCELLOR 
KONRAD ADENAUER.

SMITH. REPUBLICAN SENATE AUTHORITY ON FAR EASTERN AFFAIRS, IS THE

AL OF THE JAPANESE TREATY AND THREE RELATED PACIFIC SECURITY PACTS

HE ADDED THAT THE JAPANESE PACT "PLACES JAPAN ON A FOOTING OF EQUAL- 
ITY WITH ALL THE OTHER SOVEREIGN POWERS IN THE WORLD--WE COULD DO NO- 
LESS WITH A PROUD AND ABLE PEOPLE LIKE THE JAPANESE." 

: AT THE SAME TIME, SMITH SAID THE RELATED SECURITY TREATY, ALLOWING 
B THE U.S. AND UNITED NATIONS TO MAINTAIN TROOPS IN JAPAN, WILL GIVE 
JAPAN A "MILITARY FORCE SUFFICIENTLY STRONG TO PROTECT HERSELF." 


SMITH SAID THE THREE SECURITY TREATIES ARE NOT AS STRONG AS THE 
NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY WITH EUROPEAN NATIONS. 
UNDER THAT "AN ARMED ATTACK AGAINST ONE OR MORE OF THEM IN EUROPE 
on eeran AMERICA SHALL BE CONSIDERED AN ATTACK AGAINST THEM ALL,

THE WESTERN HEMISPHERE,®

WASHINGTON MARCH 17-(€AP)-DEVELOPMENT OF THE FIRST FULLY-AUTOMATIC 
PARACHUTING ESCAPE UNIT FOR.PILOTS FORCED TO BAIL OUT OF HIGH SPEED 
PLANES WAS DISCLOSED TODAY BY THE NAVY. 

A FURTHER PERFECTION OF THE FAMED "EJECTION SEAT," IT ELIMINATES 
THE PREVIOUS NEED OF A PILOT RELEASING HIMSELF FROM THE SEAT AND THEN 
PULLING A RIP CORD TO OPEN HIS PARACHUTE. ? 

NAVY SCIENTISTS SAID THIS WOULD ASSURE A SAFE LANDING FOR PILOTS 
WHO MIGHT "BLACK OUT" IN THE PROCESS OF BEING CATAPULTED FROM THE 
PLANE. = 

THE DEVICE, EXHIBITED FOR THE FIRST TIME AT THE 23RD ANNUAL 
INTERNATIONAL CONVER@ION OF THE AERO MEDICAL ASSOCIATION, HAS BEEN 
SUCCESSFULLY TESTED WITH HUMAN PILOTS UNDER SIMULATED FLIGHT CONDI- 
TIONS AND WITH DUMMIES EJECTED FROM PLANES FLYING AT 500 MILES AN 
HOUR. 

THE NAVY IS CURRENTLY PLANNING FIRST HUMAN TESTS IN ACTUAL FLIGHT 
AND EXPECTS TO MAKE THE EQUIPMENT STANDARD FOR THE SERVICE ACCORDING 
TO SCIENTISTS OF THE NAVL AERO MEDICAL EQUIPMENT LABORATORY AT PHILA= 
DELPHIA. THE NEW UNIT WAS DEVELOPED THERE. 

THE SEAT IS CATAPULTED FROM A PLANE WHEN THE OPERATOR PULLS A 
CORD. THEREAFTER, EVERY 

A SMALL PARACHUTE, DEPLOYED IN A FRACTION OF A SECOND AFTER 
STABILIZES THE SEAT TO. PREVENT TUMBLING. SEVERAL SECONDS 

LATER, A’PRE-SET CARTRIDGE, PLACED IN BACK OF THE SEAT, EXPLODES. | 

THIS ACTIVATES A CABLE WHICH RELEASES THE FLIER'S "LAP=BELT"--AND HE'S 


HE LEAVES THE SEAT. ANOTHER GADGET AUTOMATICALLY "ARMS" ANOTHER 


~ 


PRESSET DEVICE WHICH CONTROLS THE RELEASE OF THE FLIER'S OWN PARACHUTE. 


LLS FREE FOR FROM THREE TO FIVE SECONDS--SO AS TO GET HIM 

QUICKLY OUT OF THE AREA WHERE BREATHING MIGHT BE A PROBLEM--AND THEN 
HIS OWN PARACHUTE AUTOMATICALLY OPENS. , 

FOR EXAMPLE. IF HE BAILED OUT AT 40,000 FEET, HIS ‘CHUTE COULD BE 

+OMATICALLY AT ABOUT 12,000. BUT THE TIMING MECHANISM 

tED FOR ANY ALTITUDE, ~

UNITEDWNATIONS, MARCH 17-CAP)-A PRESS FREEDOM WATCHDOG 
COMMITTEE WAS PROPOSED TODAY TO THE U.N»SUBCOMMISSION ON FREEDOM 
OF INFORMATION BY ROBERT WALTHMAN, BRITISH EXPERT ON THE GROUP. 

WAITHMAN SAID HIS PROPOSED COMMITTEE, OF THREE TO FIVE MEMBERS, 
COULD HOLD PUBLIC INQUIRIES IN EVERY COUNTRY AND DRAMATIZE THE 
FACT THAT THE FREE PRESS BELONGS TO THE MILLIONS OF THE PEOPLE AND 
SUFFERS WHEN THE GOVERNMENT ATTEMPTS TO BECOME ITS CUSTODIAN. 

THE 12-MEMBER U.N. SUBCOMMISSION IS CHARTING FUTURE WORK IN THE 
FIELD OF INFORMATION FOR THE U.N. IT IS DUE TO GO OUT OF EXISTENCE 
WHEN IT FINISHES ITS WORK LATE THIS WEEK. BUT SALVADOR LOPEZ, OF 
THE PHILIPPINES, INTRODUCED A RESOLUTION CALLING ON THE PARENT 
ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COUNCIL TO CONTINUE THE SUBCOMMISSION, 
RESTRICTING ITS MEMBERSHIP TO WORKING JOURNALISTS.

HOSPITAL FIRE (170) 

TOKYO, MARCH 18-(AP)=FIRE OF UNKNOWN ORIGIN DAMAGED TWO WARDS OF 
A U.S. AIR FORCE HOSPITAL NEAR HERE TODAY, THE 219 PATIENTS-- 
INCLUDING 40 BED PATIENTS AND TWO NEWBORN BABIES--WERE REMOVED (O52 
WITHOUT INJURY BY AMERICAN AIRMEN AND JAPANESE CIVILIANS. “ih 

SEVERAL AIRMEN FIGHTING THE FLAMES WERE OVERCOME BY SMOKE. 

LT. COLe Le Ee GATTO, COMMANDING OFFICER OF THE HOSPITAL, SAID 
QUICK ACTION OF THE AIRMEN AND CIVILIANS SAVED MANY PATIENTS FROM 
INJURY AND KEPT THE BLAZE FROM SPREADING, 

THE BED PATIENTS AND THE BABIES WERE TRANSFERRED TO A HOSPITAL AT 
NEARBY JOHNSON BASE. THE REST OF THE PATIENTS WERE TAKEN TO A SERVICE 
CLUB, BUT WERE.RETURNED TO THE DAMAGED FAR EAST AIR FORCES* MATERIAL 
BASE HOSPITAL LATER IN THE DAY. 

HOSPITAL AUTHORITIES MADE NO ESTIMATE OF THE DAMAGE. 

THEY SAID THE TWO WARDS AND THE HOSPITAL ADMINISTRATIVE OFFICES 
WOULD BE OUT OF COMMISSION TEMPORARILY. 

THREE SURGICAL OPERATIONS HAD JUST BEEN COMPLETED WHEN THE FIRE 
BROKE OUT. NONE WAS UNDERWAY WHEN IT STARTED. THE FIRE LASTED 40 


MINUTES.
